claims.text: A history of diabetes alone is associated with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 1.9 compared with individuals without diabetes, stroke, or MI.
A history of stroke alone is associated with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 2.1 compared with reference individuals.
A history of myocardial infarction alone is associated with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 2.0 compared with reference individuals.
A history of both diabetes and myocardial infarction is associated with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 3.7 compared with reference individuals.
A history of both diabetes and stroke is associated with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 3.8 compared with reference individuals.
A history of both stroke and myocardial infarction is associated with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 3.5 compared with reference individuals.
A history of diabetes, stroke, and myocardial infarction is associated with an age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 6.9 compared with reference individuals.
At 60 years of age, a history of any two cardiometabolic conditions (diabetes, stroke, MI) is associated with 12 years of reduced life expectancy.
At 60 years of age, a history of all three cardiometabolic conditions (diabetes, stroke, MI) is associated with 15 years of reduced life expectancy.

evidence.description: In the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, HR for all-cause mortality was 1.9 (95% CI, 1.8-2.0) in participants with a history of diabetes.
In the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, HR for all-cause mortality was 2.1 (95% CI, 2.0-2.2) in participants with stroke.
In the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, HR for all-cause mortality was 2.0 (95% CI, 1.9-2.2) in participants with MI.
In the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, HR for all-cause mortality was 3.7 (95% CI, 3.3-4.1) in participants with both diabetes and MI.
In the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, HR for all-cause mortality was 3.8 (95% CI, 3.5-4.2) in participants with both diabetes and stroke.
In the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, HR for all-cause mortality was 3.5 (95% CI, 3.1-4.0) in participants with both stroke and MI.
In the Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, HR for all-cause mortality was 6.9 (95% CI, 5.7-8.3) in participants with diabetes, stroke, and MI.
Survival modeling applying ERFC HRs to contemporary US death rates showed that at age 60 years, a history of any 2 conditions was associated with 12 years of reduced life expectancy.
Survival modeling applying ERFC HRs to contemporary US death rates showed that at age 60 years, a history of all 3 conditions was associated with 15 years of reduced life expectancy.

methodologies.name: Pooled individual participant meta-analysis and life expectancy survival modeling
methodologies.description: Calculated age- and sex-adjusted hazard ratios for mortality across disease groups using Cox proportional hazards models and estimated reductions in life expectancy by applying age-specific HRs to contemporary US population death rates.

limitations.text: Few population cohorts have had sufficient power, detail, and longevity to enable comparisons of participants with multimorbidity with participants within the same cohorts without baseline conditions.
The operational definition of cardiometabolic multimorbidity did not include a history of hypertension.
The study lacked access to time-varying exposure information to update participant multimorbidity status during follow-up.
Only subsets of participants had complete information on certain covariates, such as medication use and exact dates of baseline diagnoses.

future_work.text: Elucidate explanations for sex-based differences and interactions in the association between cardiometabolic multimorbidity and mortality.
